Undulate

UN-juh-layt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To undulate to move with a smooth, wavelike motion.

The flag began to undulate slowly as the first breeze of the morning arrived.

Worked Example

Beneath the surface, a school of eels seemed to undulate in a single continuous ribbon of motion.

The eels weren't swimming in straight lines -- their bodies moved in a smooth, wavelike ripple, which is exactly what undulate describes.

How Undulate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

ripple

ripple: to move in small waves

sway

sway: to move slowly back and forth

Antonyms

stiffen

stiffen: to become rigid and unmoving

How Strong Is It? — shift → undulate → churn

shift vs. undulate

shift vs. undulate: A single shift is one small movement; to undulate is to move continuously in smooth, repeating waves.

churn vs. undulate

churn vs. undulate: Undulating water moves in gentle, even waves; churning water is violent and turbulent.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — und

root — und: wave (Latin (unda))

suffix — -ulate

suffix — -ulate: to perform an action related to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Undulate comes from Latin unda, 'wave,' plus -ulate -- so undulate literally means 'to wave.'

Use the root in a new word: inundate

Use the root in a new word: inundate: The same unda root gives us inundate -- a word you've already met earlier in this course, literally 'to be overwhelmed by waves' -- and the everyday word abundant, which originally meant 'overflowing like water,' from Latin abundare.

Root Check

Word Choice

Undulate describes physical, wavelike motion -- fields of grass, water, ribbons of fabric -- and is not typically used for emotions or moods the way many of this unit's other words are.
